entries.title: Justice Kagan Warns Supreme Court Rulings Are Fueling Polarization
entries.summary: The liberal-leaning justice said both political parties are "in a race to the bottom" with partisan gerrymanders.
entries.content:
By Lindsay Whitehurst

Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said voting and elections decisions from her conservative Supreme Court colleagues have helped make the country more politically polarized and less democratic.

In a speech two weeks before the pivotal midterm elections for control of Congress, the liberal-leaning justice sharply criticized how the majority’s rulings have affected the nation’s political environment.

“The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effect of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should,” she said during a talk before students and professors at Catholic University's law school in Washington, D.C.

She blasted rulings that weakened the Voting Rights Act and campaign finance regulations while opening the door for more partisan gerrymandering. She dissented from those decisions.

“Over the last couple of years especially, both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, … making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she said. “The people of America look around and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare, and they're right.”

The court’s majority, for its part, said in a 2019 ruling that courts drawing voting districts for maximum advantage is a political dispute and federal courts can’t step in. Conservatives have separately ruled that key campaign finance regulations violate the freedom of speech. This year, the court further narrowed protections in the Voting Rights Act, which had helped increase minority representation.

That helped feed a redistricting frenzy touched off by President Donald Trump, who is trying to hold on to the Republicans' slim House majorities in the November election.

Still, Kagan said it's unfair to say the majority reflexively supports the president. She pointed to key areas where the court has pushed back against Trump, including tariffs, birthright citizenship and mail ballots.

entries.title: Trump’s Super PACs Have Spent More Than $238 Million Since September
entries.summary: The spending spree leaves the president’s PAC network with $189 million in reserves.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s super PAC network poured about $238 million into key congressional races from September through mid-October, new federal filings show.

The aggressive fall spending spree left MAGA Inc. and two related committees, No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC, with a cumulative $189 million in reserves as of mid-October — just a few weeks after Trump claimed that he had raised close to $1 billion.

The disclosures came hours after Trump claimed on Truth Social that he had already spent more than $300 million helping Republicans ahead of the midterms and would likely spend $100 million more — figures that line up with what he said earlier this fall he anticipated spending.

Notable donors to the network of committees included real estate developer Steve Wynn, who gave $8 million; Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman with $5 million; and Wisconsin billionaire Diane Hendricks, who tossed in $5 million.

GEO Reentry Services, a company associated with operating several U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities, gave MAGA Inc. $1 million, bringing its combined contributions to more than $4 million.

The Vapor Technology Association gave $300,000. The company donated those funds on Sept. 8, and then announced a seven-figure advertising campaign Sept. 22 urging Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to rewrite Food and Drug Administration rules regarding flavored vaping products.

Trump has crisscrossed the country in recent months, holding dozens of rallies to support Republicans in competitive races. But the blitz began mainly after fellow party members publicly and privately begged the president to get more involved, and he had largely held off from dedicating serious sums from his campaign coffers until September.

From January 2025 through August, MAGA Inc. had taken in $424.4 million and paid out $32.4 million, and only about $2.5 million was reported as independent spending to elect or defeat candidates. The PAC drew scrutiny from political analysts and some Republicans for drawing large sums without spending aggressively on races that could decide control of Congress come November.

By mid-September the three groups aligned with MAGA Inc. ramped up spending, scheduling about $138 million in advertising, mail and text messaging spending across about 50 races, although much of that total was aimed for advertising reserved for the weeks ahead.

By October, the Trump-led PACs were already being forced to make choices about which Republicans to keep helping. Politico reported on Oct. 12 that MAGA Inc. planned to pull spending from several House races, including Michigan’s 8th District, and focus on protecting Senate seats in Ohio, Alaska and Iowa, all states Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Trump’s insistence that he controls the money raised by MAGA Inc. spurred a recent Federal Election Commission complaint alleging the president broke rules governing how elected officeholders can control PAC money. In August, he corrected a Punchbowl reporter who described MAGA Inc. as controlled by his allies.

“Not my allies,” he said. “I control it.”

entries.title: The State Department Is Pushing Out Senior Foreign Service Officers
entries.summary: The Trump administration is looking to replace long-tenured staff with more loyal personnel, current and former employees say.
entries.content:
The State Department is aggressively trying to force out its most senior foreign service officers, according to nine current and former staff, who suggested that Trump administration officials are seeking to cast aside veteran personnel who they view as standing in the way of their agenda.

At the same time, the current and former employees said, State is recruiting and promoting new staff who they view as more politically loyal.

“The State Department is trying to get people to quit,” said one current foreign service officer, who was granted anonymity out of fear or retribution.

This effort comes more than a year after the State Department carried out massive layoffs, hollowing out the United States’ international foreign service footprint. Those who have spent decades in the State Department have said the administration’s approach has weakened relationships abroad, and led to deficient leadership internally and less informed foreign policy decisions.

The department has shrunk the number of roles available to senior foreign servants by freezing positions or downgrading them to lower levels, the State Department personnel said.

Many top-ranked career staff have voluntarily headed to the exits as their careers are stalled. Top political staff at the department have directly asked some long-tenured personnel to retire, former employees said. They have reassigned other top career staff into the Administration Bureau, what employees consider to be a “purgatory” where employees' careers “go to die.”

“A whole lot of senior foreign service have left because there are no jobs for them,” a second current foreign service officer said.

The State Department, like the military, operates an “up-or-out” system, meaning staff could be forced out if they do not get promoted quickly enough.

The State Department laid off more than 1,300 employees last year. Senior foreign service officers were disproportionately targeted in those cuts.

Around 3,500 foreign service employees have left the State Department since President Donald Trump retook office, according to the American Foreign Service Association, and a majority of those were in the senior ranks or one level below. Departing employees who have gone through the mandatory retirement classes this year said their size had grown by orders of magnitude and the department has been forced to hold sessions more often.

Tommy Pigott, a State Department spokesperson, said The Washington Sun’s reporting validated the agency’s efforts.

"Those bureaucrats who are complaining to the press prove the point that they shouldn’t have, and can’t be, trusted with sensitive information,” Pigott said.

The department is seeking out politically aligned staff through other means. It has increasingly leaned on the Ben Franklin Fellowship — which a Trump-aligned group of current and former State officials founded in 2024 — to identify individuals to hire and promote, current and former staff said. Individuals aligned with the group are disproportionately in senior roles. Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau is one of the Ben Franklin Fellows.

“There are people who are supportive of what is happening,” said Kelly Adams-Smith, who ended her 28-year foreign service career after the Trump administration withdrew her nomination to serve as ambassador to Moldova. “They are finding, much to their surprise, very senior positions in the department.”

One person said they participated in an interview panel for a senior-level position and were told by someone close to political leadership that the process was just for show and it had been predetermined the job was going to a Ben Franklin Fellow.

Earlier this year, State awarded a $1 million, no-bid contract to a recruitment firm whose CEO has said more Christians should serve in government and hiring at the department had become too “woke.” State also added a “fidelity” section to the performance evaluation process, requiring managers to assess employees’ commitment to “completely aligning oneself and one’s team to the most current [U.S. government] goals.”

Outside the favored circles, the administration has made it more difficult for foreign service officers to climb the ranks. This fall’s bidding cycles — the process through which a large swath of the diplomatic corps find new assignments each year — have left staff with fewer senior positions available than ever before.

Roles that were typically set aside for senior foreign service officers, such as an embassy’s deputy chief of mission, have been downgraded to a lower rank. For the second year in a row, embassies have also received directives to freeze a certain number of positions. Additionally, Trump is setting aside an usually small number of ambassadorships for career staff — and nearly half of those roles remain vacant.

“It’s like musical chairs but taking chairs away faster so people wind up with nowhere to go,” said a State employee who recently left the department.

Even senior employees willing to serve in lower positions have been told they would not be selected for those roles, employees said.

The State Department confirmed that it was not prioritizing years of service for senior jobs.

The policy changes, political pressure and a wave of resignations are having a significant impact on U.S. diplomacy, the current and former staff said.

Employees now feel reluctant to offer their views on key matters, something staff described as historically fundamental to the nation’s diplomatic success. Doing so could endanger their chances of promotion or risk other efforts to sideline their careers, they said.

“People are afraid to speak out, to voice their opinions even if they believe their opinions need to be heard,” said one foreign service officer who recently left the department.

Newer employees with less experience and fewer relationships abroad are in critical positions, both because of who the Trump administration is selecting and more junior workers are less likely to feel financially secure enough to step down.

“Someone who can retire or is more economically secure is more likely to tell the emperor that the emperor has no clothes,” one of the recently departed foreign service officers said. “Junior people are more likely to just say yes.”

That will lead to less informed foreign policy decisions, the person said.

“Good policy depends on good information,” the former employee said. “If you’re not getting the good information because people are afraid to share, then you are likely to have bad policy.”

Adams-Smith noted that when experienced diplomats leave the department, the agency also loses their “networks of contacts” abroad.

She had planned to continue serving at State, but reversed course after she realized the administration was “not interested in expert advice.”

“There was no place for me and it was clear my expertise was not going to be valued or welcome,” Adams-Smith said. “With the way they were handling things, it was clear it was time to go.”

Pigott, the department spokesperson, said State is willing to hear advice from “patriotic Americans.”

"Secretary [Marco] Rubio values candid insights from patriotic Americans who have chosen to serve their country,” he said. “What we will not tolerate is people using their positions to actively undermine the duly elected president’s objectives.”

Another recently retired foreign service officer said that replacing long-tenured staff with greener employees will lead to a “10-year gap where you don’t have seasoned expertise in bilateral, multilateral and interagency contexts. That will be detrimental to American interests.”

A diplomat who recently left the department said the administration’s approach could soon lead to a crisis.

“Honest advice is not being rendered,” the former employee said. “At some point, god forbid, something is going to come back and bite them, and maybe all of us, in the behind.”

entries.title: Trump’s Campaigning in Traditional Republican Strongholds Isn’t Making His Party See Red
entries.summary: GOP strategists say they are largely happy with the president’s focus on shoring up turnout instead of contesting battleground races.
entries.content:
GREENVILLE, N.C. — President Donald Trump is doing what some didn’t expect: He’s crisscrossing the country to campaign for Republicans, spending his time — and his super PAC’s cash — to keep a blue wave from pulling the final two years of his presidency under.

The change in strategy, Trump said Tuesday night at a rally for Senate candidate Michael Whatley, was intentional.

“I'm doing something different,” he told the crowd. “I'm working like a dog, and I love being with you.”

Trump’s speech beneath a billowing American flag at a campaign rally in North Carolina was like so many others he’s given in recent weeks — one that wove together a tangle of seemingly unrelated threads rather than providing a targeted closing message for a crucial election. Instead of talking about rising consumer prices, he opined on what constitutes an attractive man, complained about election integrity and welcomed racing legend Richard Petty to talk about supporters being Trump’s “pit crew.”

But as the president storms the country to stump for candidates in the election’s closing days, his itinerary has largely focused on red states and featured nods of acknowledgment to the problems that have cratered his approval rating to historic lows and set the scene for a potential blue wave. Republicans are betting that Trump’s message matters less than his presence does.

“The rallies are working for the people that they need to work for: the base,” said Steve Bannon, Trump’s former chief strategist and the host of “War Room,” a podcast popular among Trump supporters.

Shoring up Republican turnout in traditionally red areas of the country, Bannon and other Republican operatives tell The Washington Sun, is how Trump can best serve his party during the home stretch. The president remains the best motivator for getting Republicans to vote, even as his broader popularity has faded. And with control of Congress hanging in the balance, juicing turnout is desperately needed.

“He’s firing up the base,” said Alan Powell, a Greenville-area resident at Trump’s rally Tuesday. “That’s what matters.”

Democratic candidates, super PACs and committees are pouring money into states, races and districts that Republicans won by significant margins in 2024. Democratic Senate candidates in Kansas, Nebraska and Alaska — states Trump won in 2024 by 16 percentage points, 20 points and 13 points, respectively — are leading or within striking distance of the Republican incumbents in recent polling. Democratic operatives say the party can win the Senate majority, an outcome considered almost unthinkable just two years ago.

“The problem is we’re gonna lose the House in red states,” said a conservative operative, who, like others in this story, spoke on the condition of anonymity to talk openly about campaign dynamics. “That’s fucked up.”
Trump 26289817352212 (8026x5350, AR: 1.50)Republicans believe Trump’s presence on the campaign trail is the best counter to Democratic momentum. Turnout in the midterms trends lower than in presidential election years, and that, Republican strategists say, allows Trump to affect the outcome by activating more of the people passionate enough to vote.

“The midterm elections are all about turnout, and there's no one who energizes and engages Republican voters like President Donald J. Trump,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. “Republicans are thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”

Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Bannon pointed to an increase in the number of Trump’s plane-hangar rallies, likening them to the final stretch of his 2016 campaign.

“He identifies the way to do this is to get the base,” Bannon said, adding that he’s seen a demonstrable change in urgency among Trump’s most loyal voters over the past two weeks. “Not simply the vote, but to make the list for 10 people to get them out to start canvassing, calling the phone banks.”

Trump promised in September to spend the final month of the election on the road, stumping for Republican candidates. And he has. But instead of barnstorming traditional swing states, the president has spent more time bouncing across the comfortable confines of states that should be Trump Country — Alabama, Tennessee, Kansas, Ohio, Nebraska and Alaska among them.

Trump plans to visit South Carolina, Iowa and Florida before returning to Georgia this weekend and to Texas next week. He’ll also make a rare battleground stop in Michigan.

Even the stops in more competitive states and districts have landed in friendly regions. Dalton, Georgia, the site of his rambling rally on Friday, is nestled in the district Marjorie Taylor Greene represented before she left Congress. On Tuesday, Trump visited North Carolina’s 3rd District, which overwhelmingly elected Republican Rep. Greg Murphy in 2024.

Trump’s rare forays into battlegrounds have delighted Democrats and dismayed some Republicans.

“He should stick to the White House; he should just stay there,” one Republican operative in Georgia said about Trump’s visit. “All he’s doing is hurting Republicans.”

Asked about the same rally, a Georgia Democrat was gleeful.

“If Trump could come to Georgia every week, we’d invite him,” the operative said, adding that Trump’s presence could help deliver the gubernatorial race for Keisha Lance Bottoms to make her the state’s first Black governor.
Trump 26293856909032 (8210x4618, AR: 1.78)Any impact from Trump’s rallies isn’t likely to stem from his messaging. His speeches have been long, winding variations of the same talk he’s given for months: dire warnings of coming communism brought by Democrats, a defense of the ongoing Iran war and blaming his predecessor for high prices — all mixed with pleas to act like he is on the ballot, tepid praise for whichever Republicans he is stumping for and insults for those candidates’ Democratic opponents.

Specific, state-based messaging — like using the red meat of gun-control policies while rallying in Montana — has been rare. And operatives are OK with that.

“Trump usually provides a lot of different messages,” said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean, “but everyone's used to that.”

The goal, Bonjean added, is to generate enthusiasm among the MAGA base.

“If they feel better about going to the polls because they heard from President Trump directly, then that's a win,” he said.

Trump’s visit earlier this month to Tennessee, for example, was to Montgomery County, an area that state Rep. Jeremy Faison said has felt closer to purple than red this cycle.

“Strategically, he’s trying to fit in places like that that he knows he can hopefully turn out some red voters,” Faison said.

Trump said in a Tuesday social media post that he expects to spend over $400 million by Nov. 3, seemingly referring to spending from his affiliated super PACs. He added that $300 million has already been spent, including on advertising, voter turnout and rallies.

One Democratic operative said it was smart to focus on boosting turnout within Republican strongholds rather than risking alienating swing-state voters. It showed Trump is “reading the room,” they added.

But if Trump’s trips to Georgia, North Carolina and Michigan lead to more battleground rallies, that operative said they wouldn’t be sad. Another Democratic strategist took it even further after Trump’s rally in Kansas on Monday, where he was heckled by a protester screaming, “I fucking hate you!”

“If Trump wants to stay in Kansas for the next two weeks,” the strategist said, “I wouldn’t mind!”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: The Long Way Home
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 21, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Wheelchair accessibility, the fate of “Trash Island” and a sign of life from the Commanders. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10. A touch cooler means we may fall short of 70, but another full day of sun puts us back at the brink of a perfect score. Read the full forecast.




THE LATEST

Much of Alex Graf’s life is the same now as it was before he began using a wheelchair last summer. What’s vanished is his punctuality. Now, Graf can expect to be late — late to work meetings, late to physical therapy appointments, late getting home to his wife and two toddlers.

“Being disabled is hard, but it’s mostly on other people,” he said. “You're ceding the control of your own time, and you're ceding it to people who don't care, honestly. And not people, but systems.”

Graf has taken to Instagram to vent about the Metro elevator outages and long Uber wait times that often leave him stranded around D.C., but he’s hoping to turn that anger into action, The Washington Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

First, he’s pushing for Metro to announce when coming stations have an elevator outage. Though WMATA tracks that information online, it’s not always up to date. He’s also one of many disability advocates pushing for the D.C. Council to pass a bill that would require rideshare platforms to ensure wheelchair-accessible rides arrive in no more than 110% of the average wait time for standard ones, ban drivers from refusing service to disabled people and pay 10 cents per non-accessible ride into a fund that will purchase more wheelchair-accessible vehicles.

“We should not allow companies to operate in the District while offering one service to people who walk, and a lesser one to people who roll,” Graf testified at a Monday hearing. “These are some of the largest, most sophisticated companies in the world. They can solve this. They have done it in other cities, but only when they have been required to do so. Equal access is not a stretch goal. It should be the cost of doing business here.”

Uber sent an email to D.C. users on Tuesday urging them to oppose the bill, saying it could “significantly raise the cost” of trips, Zara reports. Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau, the bill’s author, called it “fearmongering.”

“As anyone who takes ride-hailing in D.C. and elsewhere knows, the cost of trips has already been jacked up by surge pricing and other opaque algorithms,” Nadeau said in a statement to The Sun. “If fares go up, the legislation isn’t the problem; rather it’s the business model that boosts profits at the expense of drivers and customers. Even after all this time, Uber still seems to think it shouldn’t be held accountable in the way that other industries are.”








FROM THE DISTRICT

Have you ever been to Trash Island? On Tuesday, President Donald Trump used the derisive moniker to refer to East Potomac Park, where he is pushing aggressively to renovate the existing golf course. Trump said it had been “badly managed for so many decades” and that his proposed rehab project would turn it into an “Island of Beauty and Success.” Critics, though, worry that many golfers will be priced out and runners and cyclists will lose a popular destination for workouts. The fate of East Potomac Park may rest with Judge Ana Reyes, whom The Washington Post profiled this week.

D.C. police have temporarily shuttered the Capitol Hill bar where a National Guard member was shot in a gunfight Sunday night, WTOP reports. D.C. law allows the police chief to close bars or restaurants for up to 96 hours if they deem there is an imminent threat to public safety.





FROM VIRGINIA

The Fairfax County police chief defended an officer who county executive Bryan Hill said treated him disrespectfully during a traffic stop last week, ABC 7 News reports.

Hill was pulled over for a license plate violation and was seen on body-cam footage asking the officer, “Did you hear who I told you I am?” after introducing himself. Hill also called Police Chief Kevin Davis to complain that the officer “had no idea who I was,” according to an email Davis sent to the deputy county executive. Hill later apologized in a statement, saying he contacted Davis to commend the officer’s professionalism.

A premium $125 million passenger terminal is coming to Washington Dulles International Airport, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. So-called VIPs will be able to enjoy some of the on-the-ground luxuries of flying private, even if they’re commercial passengers.





FROM MARYLAND

The Supreme Court will decide a case on the role race plays in Montgomery County Public Schools’ admissions policies, and how they are challenged in court, The Sun’s Domonique King reports.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For roller skaters: “Late Skate” at Anacostia Park, Saturday.

For horse girls and boys: Kids’ Day at Washington International Horse Show, Saturday.

For Broadway buffs: “Fallen Angels” at various movie theaters, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Commanders AP - 26292860763786 (5347x3565, AR: 1.50)Things looked pretty bleak for the Commanders at halftime of Monday night’s meeting with the 49ers. Washington was down big, its slow start marked by miscues and mental mistakes. But, as The Sun’s Dave Sheinin writes, “it feels as if that second half changed everything.” The Commanders still lost, 23-17, but their late rally was inspiring enough to keep fans on the hook (and Dan Quinn on the sidelines).

Any potential turnaround will have to happen without Terry McLaurin, who will miss the rest of the season with a torn patellar tendon.

In more injury news: The Wizards will be without rookie AJ Dybantsa in tonight’s season opener against the Bucks, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. The No. 1 overall pick is still working his way back from the ankle injury he suffered in last week’s preseason finale.

The Tampa Bay Rays are headed to the World Series, and that’s good news for Nats fans. Yes, you read that correctly — Washington’s new regime is filled with former Rays employees, and Tampa Bay’s data-driven culture has had a major impact on the Nats’ new approach. In fact, one coach told The Sun’s Jesse Dougherty that sometimes it feels like the Nats are trying to “out-Rays the Rays.”

What to Watch Today

NBA: Wizards vs. Bucks, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

MLS: D.C. United at Cincinnati, 7 p.m. (Apple TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

entries.title: Morning Sun: Trump’s Travels
entries.content:
Today’s notice: All the president’s tour dates. Scoop: State Dept. diplomats are being pushed out for having the wrong politics. First look at new Everytown-DGA spending. Exclusive look at House Democrats’ latest map expansion. A sobering poll about the state of our politics. About those planes Kristi Noem bought. And: Another STOCK Act violation. 





THE LATEST

What is the president doing? Republicans have all but written off North Carolina this cycle, with the smartest people in various war rooms pulling out money and sending it to candidates in other states who could use the help. Donald Trump is going a different route — he stumped in the state last night, using some of his precious remaining campaign time in a place his party is no longer buying ads.

Trump played the optimistic cheerleader, saying that his rally-after-rally, state-by-state effort will show the doubters that Republicans can still win. “I’m working like a dog, and I love being with you,” he said.

The Washington Sun’s Jasmine Wright was at the rally, which featured a giant, billowing American flag. Today she has a story with our Ben T.N. Mause about how Trump’s quixotic campaign choices are playing among the strategists in D.C. “He should stick to the White House; he should just stay there,” one Republican strategist said. “All he’s doing is hurting Republicans.”

Trump veterans see a plan to save the day in places where the GOP is floundering. “He identifies the way to do this is to get the base,” Steve Bannon told The Sun. “Not simply the vote, but to make the list for 10 people to get them out to start canvassing, calling the phone banks.”

While most Democrats give a big thumbs up to Trump’s travel schedule, loving every second that the unpopular president is in these states, there are some who see a method to this presidential GOTV push. With his approval rating in the 30s, there are truly challenging things for Trump, like wooing independents, and things that might be easier, like trying to wake up MAGA again. One Democratic operative said it was a smart strategy to focus on boosting turnout in Republican strongholds rather than risking alienating swing-state voters. It showed Trump is “reading the room,” they said.

How it sounded in Greenville: The president ran through his greatest hits — $5,000 checks! Immigrant crime! Sen. Jon Husted’s ass! — and some goodies for the North Carolina locals: Two new semiconductor plants, including a $1.5 billion investment from the “Department of War.”

The crowd, huddled on a chilly tarmac, seemed most enthusiastic about the ejection of a smattering of protestors, Jasmine reports, with some in MAGA hats saluting their exit with the double bird. NASCAR legend Richard Petty helped close out the rally, calling Trump the best driver the country has ever had and that it was time to help pick him the “best pit crew.”

More: Trump’s Super PACs Have Spent More Than $238M Since September • Justice Kagan Warns Supreme Court Rulings Are Fueling Polarization • Dick Durbin Wants to ‘Walk Out’ the Front Door After 44 Years in Congress • Social Security Fixes Millions of Records After Trump’s Fraud Claims Fade Away






FROM FOGGY BOTTOM 


Scoop: Ideological replacements of career diplomats. The State Department is aggressively trying to push out its most senior foreign service officers while recruiting and promoting new staff viewed as more politically loyal, The Sun’s Eric Katz reports. The department is asking senior diplomats to retire, demoting them and shrinking opportunities for them.

Senior leaders have increasingly leaned on the Ben Franklin Fellowship — a two-year-old Trump-aligned group of current and former State officials — to identify individuals to hire and promote. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau is one of the Ben Franklin Fellows. Tommy Pigott, a department spokesperson, defended the moves: “Those bureaucrats who are complaining to the press prove the point that they shouldn’t have, and can’t be, trusted with sensitive information.”

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


First on The Sun: New gun-safety group spending. Everytown for Gun Safety Action Fund and Victory Fund and the Democratic Governors Association are dropping another $3 million into digital ads for state-level races in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada and Wisconsin as Democrats fight for governorships and trifecta control in these states, The Sun’s Elena Schneider tells us. The ad buys come on the heels of Michael Bloomberg’s announcement that he’d be pumping in $80 million into Democrats’ midterm efforts, including through the DGA and Everytown.

Exclusive: Democrats’ bullish predictions. The House Majority PAC told donors in a private memo shared with Elena that seats Trump won by up to 21 percentage points are now within margin-of-error range for a flip. More cash could help make those dreams come true, the memo outlines: “Our polling shows that Democrats can compete in these districts, but translating that potential into additional victories will require resources to reach voters and make the case against vulnerable Republicans in the final sprint to Election Day.”

Reminder: The stakes are very high this midterm. According to a new poll from Gallup out this morning, just 43% of adults say “the federal government is effective at making a positive impact on people’s lives.” That’s an 8 point drop from last year. The poll shows a 49-point gap between the share of Americans who believe the federal government has the power to make a difference and those who say it’s actually doing it. That ambivalence toward the idea that elected officials can actually do anything of note sets a high bar for whomever wins. Add restore faith in government ever accomplishing things to the long agenda for any incoming Congress.

More: Susan Collins’ New Strategy: Sounding a Lot Like Her Democratic Opponent • James Talarico Campaign to Super PACs: Highlight Anti-Paxton Republicans

FROM DHS


Scoop: Kristi Noem plane fleet update. The purchase of several aircraft by the Department of Homeland Security during the final days of the former secretary’s tenure is tied to an “ongoing criminal law enforcement investigation,” the department’s Privacy Office told The Sun’s Mark Alfred. The acknowledgement was made as part of the department’s denial of an Oct. 14 FOIA request, and post-publication of Mark’s story, DHS said the response was “sent in error.”





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Stocking up on STOCK Act violations: Rep. Laurel Lee (R-Florida) has violated the STOCK Act’s disclosure deadline for the second time this year by failing to properly report her husband’s sale of up to $100,000 in Bank of America stock, The Sun’s Dave Levinthal tells us. During a congressional STOCK Act hearing last year, Lee said Congress should “seriously consider” an “outright prohibition” on stock trading by federal lawmakers and their immediate family. Lee’s office acknowledged a request for comment but didn’t otherwise respond.

entries.title: A Major Democratic Super PAC Begs Donors for More Cash as the Map Expands
entries.summary: House Majority PAC sees surprising new opportunities for Democrats, if they can afford to run at them.
entries.content:
The flagship Democratic House super PAC is urging donors to pony up more cash in the final sprint before the midterms, pointing to private polling showing a slew of deep-red House seats within the party’s reach.

House Majority PAC told donors in a private memo, shared with The Washington Sun, that recent polling “shows that with additional resources, even more expansion seats are within reach.” The memo included polling data from 13 districts that President Donald Trump won by 8 to 21 percentage points in 2024, all of which shows those congressional races now in margin-of-error fights.

The memo is the latest evidence of Democrats’ increasing bullishness about their chance to retake the House — and the financial constraints they’re facing to capitalize on it. Last week, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee made a similar plea to donors, arguing that “we could be leaving winnable races on the table without further investment from the DCCC,” according to a copy of the memo seen by The Sun.

HMP is now making a similar donor pitch: “Our polling shows that Democrats can compete in these districts, but translating that potential into additional victories will require resources to reach voters and make the case against vulnerable Republicans in the final sprint to Election Day.”

Democrats have for months warned of a fundraising disadvantage against Republicans, saying in early September that the GOP’s financial edge could blunt Republicans’ deteriorating political environment. That disparity is felt most acutely when comparing the Republican National Committee’s $97 million cash on hand to the Democratic National Committee’s $4 million, when factoring in outstanding debt. Trump’s allied super PACs have spent nearly $200 million on campaign advertising since September, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, and the president said in a Truth Social post that he planned to spend $400 million on the campaign.

But House Democratic candidates have held their own in fundraising, frequently outraising their GOP counterparts. HMP, too, raised a record-breaking $230 million in the third quarter, but the PAC is pushing for more.

The polling described in HMP’s memo found Democratic candidates leading by at least 1 percentage point in six of the districts, offering up more evidence for the shifting House battlefield. That’s reflected in TV ad reservation changes, too. Last week, the House GOP-aligned super PAC Congressional Leadership Fund canceled its defensive spending for Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) and Tom Kean Jr. (R-New Jersey). On Tuesday, the DCCC added spending in three districts in Arizona, Ohio and South Carolina that Trump won handily in 2024.

The polling memo spotlighted several under-the-radar races.

Take Missouri’s 2nd District, which Trump won by 8 percentage points in 2024. The HMP memo said its polling found Rep. Ann Wagner (R-Missouri) down by 1 point to Democrat Fred Wellman, who outraised Wagner last quarter. On Tuesday, CLF went up with a $650,000 ad buy to boost Wagner, according to AdImpact. HMP is not yet spending in the race.

Another example comes in North Carolina, where the memo said it found Rep. Richard Hudson, the National Republican Congressional Committee chair, up by only 4 percentage points over his Democratic challenger, Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator and veteran. Hudson started airing TV ads earlier this month. Trump won Hudson’s district by 16 percentage points in 2024.

Of the districts polled in the memo, HMP is already spending in six of the districts, including Kentucky’s 6th District and Florida’s 13th District, both of which Trump won by double digits.

CORRECTION: An earlier version of this story misstated the poll finding in Missouri's 2nd District. The poll found Wagner down 1 point.

entries.title: What Does it Mean for Data Centers to Pay a Fair Share?
entries.summary: Congress’ permitting bill offers the most aggressive proposal yet to charge data centers for their power usage.
entries.content:
Almost everyone agrees that data centers should pay their fair share — even data center developers. The newest proposal out of Congress poses the question: What’s fair?

Congress has put forward its most aggressive proposal yet to protect electricity prices from massive new data center developments. The bipartisan permitting reform bill would allow utilities to charge data centers more than other customers for using the grid and would let states charge data centers more on top of that.

“I think policymakers are seeing an opportunity for a good deal to take place here between extremely wealthy technology companies and regular everyday consumers, where the technology companies put many tens of billions of dollars into the power system to pay for the upgrade and keep the costs off of everybody else,” said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies, a firm that focuses on integrating clean energy into the power grid.

The bill errs on the side of “over-collection,” Gramlich said, meaning data centers could pay more than their impact on the system and effectively subsidize other customers.

So far, major data center developers seem to be on board — though as negotiations continue things could change.

“There are many devils in the details,” Gramlich said. “Regulators at the state and federal levels will have a lot of work to do.”

The data center provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would change a longstanding federal policy that allows utilities to charge customers only one of two costs: the general “embedded” costs of operating on the energy grid or the “incremental” cost of any grid upgrades necessary to serve a new project.

Utilities usually only charge customers the embedded cost of operating on the grid, Gramlich said. Incremental costs are difficult to calculate and can vary widely based on the kinds of grid upgrades that are needed at the time a new customer is coming onboard.

Data centers, cryptocurrency miners and other “high-density computing facilities” would be subject to both of those costs together under the bill. A white paper created for utility company Exelon Corporation earlier this year found that data centers could still shift costs onto other customers if they were only charged the “incremental” costs without the continued embedded cost charges.



The bill would also require data centers and similar facilities to provide financial guarantees before the grid is upgraded and to continue paying grid costs even if they abandon projects early.

The bill also notes that states could charge data center customers extra, beyond the incremental and embedded grid costs, using the proceeds as rebates for others on the grid. It also tells states they could choose which projects can connect to the grid first based on how much extra money they’re willing to spend to subsidize other customers.

The idea of data center developers paying for the cost of upgrading the grid for their projects has been widely embraced; several of the data center provisions in the permitting bill seem directly related to President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

But past attempts to avoid shifting data center costs onto the general public have included only voluntary commitments. The permitting bill would turn that directive into law.

Despite the new potential costs, the data center and AI industries have been quiet and moderately supportive of the permitting reform bill, highlighting the support for energy and infrastructure projects from the bill as a whole.

Staci Pies, senior vice president of government affairs and policy at Incompas, an AI infrastructure association, said data center companies have “been very clear” that they will bear appropriate costs.

“They’ll contribute their fair share of whatever kind of incremental infrastructure costs are necessary in order to increase and upgrade the grid,” she said.

But, she added, the costs and analysis “needs to be transparent” — particularly if states decide to charge data centers above the embedded and incremental costs.

“In some instances data centers are going to say ‘we're willing to live by this additional charge so long as it's transparent and we understand the implications.’ And in other instances, they may not,” she said.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta didn’t respond to requests for comment on whether they supported the bill’s data center provisions. Lobbying disclosures show the Data Center Coalition spent $480,000 on lobbying between July and September, including on the permitting reform bill.

Michele Nellenbach, vice president of federal affairs at the Data Center Coalition, said the organization was still reviewing details of the bill and noted members were “investing hundreds of billions of dollars in the U.S. annually to build America’s digital infrastructure.”

Some progressives have aired concerns that the bill as a whole would amount to a giveaway for data centers because of the easing of environmental laws and the provisions to limit legal challenges to projects.

At the same time, there’s been concern that the proposed changes amount to overcharging data centers for grid connection. Travis Fisher, director of energy and environmental policy studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, wrote the bill’s data center provisions risk “shifting costs in the opposite direction,” which, he says, might be necessary to counter the opposition to AI infrastructure developments.

Over the course of the last year, data center development has faced an incredible rise in political pushback. Communities across the country have rallied against the centers being built in their backyards out of fear of higher utility costs, pollution and other concerns. Data center developers have responded by leveling up efforts to sweeten the deal for communities.

But as they scramble for access to reliable energy, developers have increasingly started running their operations off the grid, using their own power systems that don’t necessarily have any benefit for nearby communities.

Pies, with Incompas, said data center companies are using off-grid power as an “immediate solution to an immediate problem,” but want to connect to the grid as a long-term solution. The big-picture impacts of the permitting bill — more power, quicker grid upgrades and increased transmission capacity — are a critical part of that.

How much a financial burden they’re willing to shoulder, however, remains to be seen.

While the future of the bipartisan bill is uncertain, Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, said the extent of Congress’ proposal shows just how significant a demand data centers are introducing to the nation’s infrastructure.

“There's really no parallels to these data centers because they use so much energy and there's so many of them coming on so fast that I don't think we can really look to historical practice for analogous situations,” he said.

entries.title: The Rays Are in the World Series. That’s a Nats Story, Too.
entries.summary: Washington’s general manager, manager and bench coach are all former Rays employees.
entries.content:
The Rays, who just advanced to face the Brewers in the World Series, used to employ three people who now have major roles with the Nationals: general manager Ani Kilambi, manager Blake Butera and bench coach Michael Johns.

Kilambi, who started with the Rays as an intern, spent seven years with the team, ascending to assistant director of research and development. Butera was drafted by the Rays, transitioned to managing in the low-level of the minors by his mid-20s, then eventually oversaw player development. Johns was with the Rays from 2008 to 2025, spending a bulk of that time in player development, including a decade as a minor league manager.

To take the connections a step further, Shawn O’Malley, the Nationals’ assistant hitting coach, was drafted by the Rays in 2006. Beyond that, many higher-ups, including Paul Toboni, the Nats’ president of baseball operations, have worked for people who were once in the Rays’ data-obsessed brain trust. And then there’s the general idea that, as the Nationals keep building their new operation, the goal is to live on the cutting edge, which the Rays have helped make popular by winning so damn much.

In late September, a Nationals coach told me: “Process-wise, it sometimes feels like we are trying to out-Rays the Rays.”

For any fan base, that could land in a few different ways. Even before they made this World Series, the Rays’ long run of success was undeniable, especially given that their 2026 payroll ranked 25th among 30 teams (a usual spot for them). But if part of the deal is doing more with far less spending than most competitive clubs, that could be a red flag for fans, in D.C. or otherwise, who want their team to be smart — dogged and progressive in the search for any edge — while also investing in big salaries for premium talent.

None of this is to say the Nats are aiming to be a spitting image of the Rays of recent years. The Red Sox of recent years are probably more instructive. Toboni came from Boston, as did Devin Pearson, his assistant GM in charge of player development. Justin Horowitz, Toboni’s assistant GM for all player acquisitions, was with them in Boston, too, before a short stint with the Pirates, as was Andrew Wright, now a special assistant to Toboni in Washington.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

For a few seasons, Chaim Bloom, once a top exec with the Rays, was their boss in Boston, which just shows how much the Rays’ approach has spread across the sport. But when it comes to what the specific Nats-Rays connections might mean in practice, I keep thinking back to a conversation I had long before Toboni and Butera were leading the team.

Remember the Blake Snell game? Or, more specifically, remember the Blake Snell decision? As far as ways to explain the Rays and their influence on modern baseball, it remains a pretty good one.

In Game 6 of the 2020 World Series, Snell, then a starting pitcher for the Rays, had the Dodgers in knots. Through five innings, he had allowed one hit and no runs while striking out nine. The Rays led 1-0. But after Austin Barnes poked a one-out single in the sixth, Kevin Cash, the Rays’ manager, pulled Snell at just 73 pitches. The next batter, Mookie Betts, doubled off Snell’s replacement, reliever Nick Anderson. Then the game unraveled on the Rays, ending with the Dodgers winning 3-1 to take the title. This was all anyone in baseball could talk about.

For months, whenever I called a Nats coach or executive, I started with Cash’s controversial move. It was something of a bellwether for how someone felt about the direction of the sport. Broadly, old-school traditionalists viewed it as everything wrong with the analytics era, which now included the marginalization of the starting pitcher. On the other end of the spectrum, Cash’s defenders hammered the statistical validity of the decision, mostly pointing to the risk of having Snell face the Dodgers’ best hitters a third time. As ever, existing in the gray area wasn’t fashionable.

But in the winter after that World Series, on a call in January 2021, one member of the Nats’ front office made me think beyond the Rays vs. purists debate. Pulling Snell, they argued, wasn’t the most interesting part of the situation. The most interesting part was that, in the biggest moment of the season, Cash could zag from longstanding convention at all — a sign, they reasoned, of a coaching staff and front office being on the exact same page. Cash didn’t have to worry about losing his job, they added. (He remains the Rays’ manager to this day.) And to that end, this person told me, it was the kind of choice that is baked over months — years, even — because that’s what it takes to do something subversive when a title is on the line, no matter how much the numbers might have backed it up.

I was skeptical of the analysis, mostly because, from the outside, it felt impossible to tell the difference between a collaborative game plan and strict orders from Cash’s bosses. And if Cash was simply doing what the front office said, how would job security factor into this specific situation? That felt like a stretch.

But if you take the theory at face value, it does describe an ideal of organization alignment, which is something the Nats’ new leaders talk a lot about. The Rays had seemingly built a culture in which that was an organizational decision, something they would (and could) all live with because they believed in their process.

Six years later, it seems that’s where the Nats are headed, if they’re not already there. That doesn’t mean that, in a similar spot, Butera will make a decision along the same lines as pulling Snell. For one, a handful of rule changes have made it harder for teams to steal the most Rays-y elements of the Rays’ rise (restrictions on defensive shifting, the three-batter minimum rule for relievers, roster limitations, etc.). Plus, in the time since Cash yanked Snell in that Game 6, wonky, analytics-based strategy has become much more mainstream, including in Washington.

But when the Nats leaders stress the importance of top-down alignment — and they do, quite often — I think that kind of unbending trust in the process is what they’re getting at, among other hopes and dreams. Like it or not, Tampa developed a clear identity, an ethos of trying to win on the margins in unorthodox ways. Then, most importantly, they’ve stuck with it, sometimes in the face of loud public criticism. That feels aspirational for any modern operation, especially one with so many Rays-influenced folks in important positions.

entries.title: He’s Adapted to a Wheelchair. He Wishes D.C. Would, Too.
entries.summary: Alex Graf and other disability advocates are supporting a bill that would improve their access to rideshare.
entries.content:
Alex Graf is getting used to the idea that he’s no longer a punctual guy.

The rapid onset of a disorder affecting his spinal cord last summer forced the 36-year-old to transition from walking and running around his Takoma Park neighborhood to using a 400-pound powerchair. Now, Graf can expect to be late — late to work meetings, late to physical therapy appointments, late getting home to his wife and two toddlers.

“Being disabled is hard, but it’s mostly on other people,” he said. “You're ceding the control of your own time, and you're ceding it to people who don't care, honestly. And not people, but systems.”

There’s one elevator at the Takoma Station Metro. Until last year, Graf could count on a reliable commute to Gallery Place each morning on the Red Line. Metro is still the best way to get around D.C., he said — indeed, the system is often lauded as one of the world’s most accessible for wheelchair users.

“It is accessible when functional,” he said. “If that elevator goes down, you're out of luck.”
When that happens, there’s no good solution. Either Graf tracks down the station manager and arranges for a Metro Access ride to the next closest station — which typically takes an hour — or he orders a wheelchair-accessible Uber (Lyft doesn’t offer accessible rides in D.C.).
AlexGraf_wheelchair_101926_0116.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)“It's barely a service,” he said of Uber. “The last 20 times I've tried to take rideshare, I've had five successful trips, which renders it useless. If you'[ve] got 25% odds of being able to go somewhere, you may not get there, but are you really going to chance it to get back?”

Those frustrations drove Graf and his wife, Nina, to testify before the D.C. Council on Monday on a bill that would require rideshare platforms to ensure wheelchair-accessible rides arrive in no more than 110% of the average wait for standard rides, ban drivers from refusing service to disabled people, and pay 10 cents per non-accessible ride for a fund that would purchase more wheelchair-accessible vehicles, or WAVs.

“Seeing his time not respected, and frankly, our kids having to wait on him, has been horrible. It’s just straight up unfair,” said Nina. “They need to make a change. I think this bill is a great step in the right direction.”

***
Alex and Nina, who both work on health care policy issues, met in 2015 on OkCupid. The dating website rated them as an almost 100% compatibility match. They both attended the University of Wisconsin as undergraduates but had never met. They individually moved to D.C. more than a decade ago. After meeting and dating for three years, they moved to Takoma Park together in 2018 and got married the following year. They now have a 1-year-old daughter and a 3-year-old son.

Life is much the same for the couple as it was before Alex began using a wheelchair. They still have the same jobs, home, kids and commute. The same hobbies and interests.

“A lot of people say something along the lines of, ‘Man, I can't imagine being you, having young kids and a disabled husband.’ It's like, we have a lot of fun! We are adapting,” Nina said. “There's things that are really hard, but we're the same people. It's not the disability itself, it's the systems that are the most painful for us to adapt to.”

Take Monday, when the couple tried to access the Wilson Building to testify on the rideshare bill. Unable to scale the grand stairs at the building’s main entrance, Alex entered via a ramp at a side entrance. There, a security guard waved a wand over Alex’s powerchair to clear him for entry but told Nina she’d have to leave her husband and go through the main entrance.
AlexGraf_wheelchair_101926_0863.jpg (7685x5123, AR: 1.50)“That's a great example of just what it's been like to adapt. We have to separate,” said Nina, striding toward the steps at the entrance.

She waited for him on the fifth floor, outside the hearing room.

“It just feels sad,” she said. “I just want to be with my husband.”

***
Alex has lived in the D.C. area since 2012, but in the last year, he’s come to see it with new eyes. Or, perhaps, to see it for what it always was.

“I just had no idea any of this was a problem,” he said. “And then, you're living it.”

He began sharing his frustrations on an Instagram page, but he wants to convert that anger into action. One of his ideas is to have Metro announce when an upcoming station has an elevator outage. WMATA tracks them online and supplies email updates, but those aren’t always up to date. Alex has been left stranded on the platform many times — particularly at Gallery Place, the station closest to his work, where multiple elevators need to be functioning in order for him to both cross the platform and exit. WMATA did not respond to a request for comment on whether it could implement such announcements.

His other idea: improve door-to-door wheelchair-accessible transit options including rideshare, taxicabs and city paratransit. As Alex discovered on Monday, plenty of people share his view.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

He and Nina stopped at the Pret A Manger on F Street ahead of the 9:30 a.m. hearing to pick up coffees. They found three disabled women enjoying their beverages at a long, communal table — also gearing up to testify.

They swapped horror stories. One woman had waited for hours for Metro Access to pick her up after Sunday church service just the day before. Another, Heidi Case, encouraged Alex to give the council as much data as he could on how many rides had canceled on him.

“That is one of the big pushes in our testimony: data,” said Case. “It sells to government, and it creates lawsuits.”
AlexGraf_wheelchair_101926_0715.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)It was fun to be around other people with disabilities, Alex said. Especially this group: smart, supportive, self-assured. When they reached the hearing room, Case had council aides clear a couple rows of chairs for them. They deserved to be up front. As the hearing got underway, and wheelchair users took the microphone to testify, Alex and Nina continued to swap looks, share nods, drop jaws. They weren’t alone.

When one person testified about the mental load of needing to constantly monitor web pages and apps for Metro elevator outages, they weren’t alone. When another laughed off Uber and Lyft’s arguments that they are technology, not transportation, companies, and so don’t need to offer accessible rides, they weren’t alone.

“How do you respond to industry concerns that it would not be possible to provide 100% equal service?” asked Ward 1 D.C. Council member Brianne Nadeau, who introduced the bill, to one group of people testifying.

“I would like to ask them, why? Because other places do, and I don't think they're in a different universe or have different financial systems or physics,” responded Kelly Mack, a wheelchair user and accessibility advocate.

“What do you think is an appropriate timeline for WAV compliance?” the council member asked.

“I kind of think 20 years ago?” Mack quipped.

They laughed; they weren’t alone.
AlexGraf_wheelchair_101926_1067.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)AlexGraf_wheelchair_101926_1188.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)When Alex testified, he led with the data. He talked about how in the parallel universe that was 15 months ago, he could easily get picked up by these same Ubers in three or four minutes. He could book rides ahead, which is an impossibility when requesting WAVs.

“We should not allow companies to operate in the District while offering one service to people who walk, and a lesser one to people who roll,” he testified. “These are some of the largest, most sophisticated companies in the world. They can solve this. They have done it in other cities, but only when they have been required to do so. Equal access is not a stretch goal. It should be the cost of doing business here.”

Representatives from both Uber and Lyft testified opposing the bill. Their primary argument is that since drivers are contractors with their own vehicles, the companies can’t be responsible for a lack of WAV service. Instead, the city should work on increasing its supply of WAVs and then contract with their platforms. Waymo and other autonomous vehicle companies made a similar argument in a recent public hearing.

“There needs to be better WAV access; we don’t believe this bill does it,” Briana Gilmore, Uber’s head of global accessibility policy, told The Washington Sun.

If D.C. modernized its taxicabs’ payment platforms, Uber could contract with wheelchair-accessible cabs, Gilmore said. Since 20% of the city’s cab fleets have to be accessible by law, taxis currently offer the most WAVs. The city could also allow paratransit to contract with rideshare services, Gilmore added.

The bill proposes charging rideshare companies 10 cents per non-accessible ride to fund the development of more WAVs. Uber sent emails to customers Tuesday saying that any fee could be passed on to them directly, according to an email reviewed by a Sun reporter.

“The bill would penalize platforms for trips no accessible vehicle is available to take, which won’t add a single WAV to the road. Instead, we should better study the current WAV landscape in the District to best understand riders’ accessibility needs and how providers can better meet them,” a Lyft spokesperson said in a statement shared with The Sun.

Advocates, on the other hand, want to strengthen the bill and even increase that fee. Nina pushed for real enforcement — something that would ensure disabled riders get picked up quickly and are not discriminated against — and a timeline to roll these initiatives out.

Until then, she and Alex will be waiting.

“In July, Alex waited two hours for an Uber to get home from work. [My son] asked when his dad would finally be home. I explained his dad was still waiting for a ride home, and my son asked why,” she said, in testimony that moved Nadeau to tears. “How do you explain discrimination and that level of unfairness to my 3-year-old?”
AlexGraf_wheelchair_101926_0583.jpg (7564x5042, AR: 1.50)The kids miss their dad when he has to go through separate security screenings or building entrances, or when he comes home late, but ultimately, Nina said, the chair doesn’t make much of a difference to them. They ride in Alex’s lap to day care each morning. Last Halloween, just a couple months after Alex began using his powerchair, their 3-year-old dressed as a wheelchair-accessible van to go trick-or-treating — a cardboard box with a wheelchair symbol and Maryland plates.

“You see things from the perspective of kids, and it really changes you, too. Kids adapt,” Nina said. “They see joy.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Soccer Players of Week 8
entries.summary: This week’s group features a heroic defender from Bowie and a capable keeper from Magruder.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

Playoff soccer is suddenly right around the corner, and with the D.C. area’s top teams looking to close out the regular season on a high note, here are six players who got the job done in Week 8:

Luke Beglis, Senior, Defender, The Heights

The Heights has faced a gauntlet of local contenders throughout its busy regular-season schedule and has kept stacking wins. The undefeated Cavaliers have established themselves as the team to beat in the DMV, with impressive wins over Gonzaga, St. John’s, St. Albans and Churchill.

Much of the team’s regular-season success is thanks to its dominant back line, led by Beglis at the centerback position. Coach Colin Gleason’s team has allowed just nine goals all season. Last week, Beglis helped The Heights take down both Gonzaga and St. John’s to move to a flawless 14-0.

“[Beglis] is the textbook defender. … He’s so good you don’t even notice him,” Gleason said. “He’s really solid out of the air, but he’ll also connect a 40-yard pass on the ground to a forward. …He’s been just dynamite.”

Lauren Cunningham, Senior, Goalkeeper, Magruder

Cunningham has been dominant in goal all season for the Magruder girls. In just nine games, the Stony Brook commit has racked up 44 saves and allowed just four goals, posting six clean sheets. Last week, she made 15 saves and allowed one goal as the Colonels took down Einstein and Richard Montgomery.

A cerebral talent, Cunningham has also experimented playing in the field for coach Nikki Prachar’s team. She scored hat tricks against Springbrook and Rockville, flashing her offensive prowess in addition to her defensive abilities.

Harper Lewis, Junior, Defender, Good Counsel

The Good Counsel girls scored big wins last week against Whitman, Bishop McNamara and Bishop O’Connell. Lewis, a starting center back, helped the Falcons to shutout victories over the Vikings and Mustangs. She was also a pivotal part of her team’s comeback win over the Knights — after conceding two early goals, Good Counsel’s defense held strong and its offense capitalized on two late chances to earn a 3-2 victory against one of the most potent offenses in the Washington Catholic Athletic Conference.

“[Lewis] is lights out. … She basically led our defense throughout the second half,” coach Jim Bruno said. “We limited the amount of touches they had later in the game, and our defense rose to the occasion.”

Claire Radanovic, Senior, Midfield, Potomac School

The Potomac School girls, looking for their fifth straight Independent School League tournament title this fall, are surging with the playoffs around the corner. The Panthers are unbeaten in October and last week picked up a 4-2 road victory over Georgetown Day.

After the Panthers fell into an early 1-0 hole in the first 15 minutes, Radanovic’s stellar play in the midfield helped the offense find its groove in a four-goal outburst.

“Claire took over vocally, and her presence in the midfield changed the entire tone of the game,” coach Ross McEwen said. “Everything was positive, everything was smart with winning balls in the air. … She was a huge spark for our team.”

Brandon Reyes, Senior, Defender, Bowie

Hours before Bowie’s biggest regular-season game against county rival Parkdale, Bulldogs coach Frantz Deetjen assumed his team would have to play without one of its starting defenders — Reyes, nursing an ankle injury, was a gametime decision.

“I don’t miss games, Coach,” Reyes told Deetjen before the game.

Reyes got the start and was an invaluable part of the Bulldogs’ 2-0 upset win. The senior helped shut out a Parkdale offense that had scored at least four goals in each of its previous five matches.

“[Reyes] had two defining clearances when they were in on goal,” Deetjen said. “They had a breakaway down the right-hand side and he came in with a beautiful tackle. … Everyone was just gasping for air.”

Ade Sodeinde, Junior, Forward, St. Andrew’s

Sodeinde was the go-to offensive threat for St. Andrew’s last week against Bishop Ireton. In a 3-0 shutout win, the junior forward scored two goals to cap a strong week for coach Neill Ouska’s Lions.

St. Andrew’s picked up a comfortable 4-1 win over Maret earlier in the week. With the Mid-Atlantic Athletic Conference tournament right around the corner, Sodeinde and the Lions look to be real contenders.

Embassy of the Czech Republic, 3900 Spring of Freedom St. NW, 6 p.m. and 8 p.m., free, registration required

The Czech Embassy redefines diplomatic scare at its fourth annual Halloween gathering. Introduce kids to the Headless Knight, Forest Demon and Water Goblin at this combined story time and forest walk through the darkened embassy grounds. Cauldrons will also be bubbling, courtesy not of witches but The Science Guys, who conduct hands-on experiments in honor of spooky season.

DMV One-Day Choir at the George Washington Masonic National Memorial

101 Callahan Drive, Alexandria, 6:30 to 9:30 p.m., donations requested

For those who will always love Dolly Parton, show choirs and a room with great reverb, the Gaia Music Collective hosts a sing-along where participants will be assigned parts, form a choir and film a video of “I Will Always Love You,” all in one night. Going viral isn’t guaranteed, but having a good time harmonizing is.

More to explore: Emei’s “Night at the Opera” tour comes to the Lincoln Theatre

Friday


“Are You Now or Have You Ever Been?” at Arena Stage

1101 Sixth St. SW, 8 p.m., $97 to $117

“Theater to make the blood boil” is how a New York Times critic praised Eric Bentley’s play about the House Un-American Activities Committee when this show opened off Broadway in June. A very similar staging — a less starry cast but still helmed by Juilliard dean Anna Shapiro — opens at Arena Stage on Thursday and runs through Dec. 6.

Avery, Gottlieb and Rothko: By the Sea opens at The Phillips Collection

1600 21st St. NW, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., preview free for members; $20 for public starting Saturday

Three seminal artists of the mid-20th century savored spending their summers on the North Shore of Massachusetts, where they painted and, presumably, ate lots of fried quahog clams. Now the Phillips has gathered more than 90 paintings, drawings and watercolors by Milton Avery, Adolph Gottlieb and Mark Rothko into one groundbreaking show, including some works never publicly exhibited. The exhibition is open to members Thursday and Friday, while general public entrance begins on Saturday.

More to explore: Art Bites gallery talk at the Smithsonian Museum of American Art

Saturday


Kids’ Day at Washington International Horse Show
Prince George’s Equestrian Center, 14900 Pennsylvania Ave., Upper Marlboro, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., free

Gone are the days when Sixth Street NW closed down to become the Washington International Horse Show stable. Since 2022, the annual elite competition has been held at Prince George’s Equestrian Center. While less Metro-accessible, at least there is less manure downtown? Kids’ Day activities include pony rides, a hobby-horse jumping course and pony kissing booth. For $10, adults can stay to watch a Grand Prix jumping competition at 1 p.m. (Kids are free.)

The Revada Arts Center grand opening

340 Maple Drive SW, 11 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., free

Two homeless performing-arts companies and an independent cinema are moving in together in Southwest D.C. Theater Alliance, IN Series and 4EYE Film Center celebrate the opening of the Revada Arts Center with a community open house. The day kicks off at 11 a.m. with a sing-along screening of “Frozen.” Tours and other family-friendly activities continue through the afternoon.

More to explore: Final “Late Skate” of the season at Anacostia Park

Sunday


“In Search of Home” sung by the Choral Arts Society of Washington

Church of the Epiphany, 1317 G St. NW, 5 p.m., $60

The Kennedy Center’s closing has displaced not only the venue’s resident ensembles but also other DMV arts groups that have long rented out the Concert Hall and other spaces. Rather pointedly, the Choral Arts Society of Washington has titled its first concert of its itinerant 2026/27 season “In Search of Home” and programmed music about “humanity, displacement and belonging” by Bernstein, Brahms and Buxtehude.

“Fallen Angels” 

Screenings of the Broadway play at various theatres; times and prices vary

Rose Byrne (“Bridesmaids”) and Kelli O’Hara (“The Gilded Age”) both earned Tony nominations for their performances in the 1925 Noël Coward show briefly revived on Broadway in the spring. On Thursday and Sunday, area movie theaters will screen a version captured for Broadway HD. DMV viewing options include AFI Silver, Alamo Drafthouse and the Angelika Film Center in Merrifield.
