entries.title: Dick Durbin Wants to ‘Walk Out’ the Front Door After 44 Years in Congress
entries.summary: The longest-serving Democratic Whip put the Dream Act on the map but leaves without its passage.
entries.content:
Sen. Richard J. Durbin spent more than two decades advising Democratic leaders what to do. But his most important recommendation might have come 20 years ago at Chicago’s Union League when he pulled aside his junior colleague for some advice.

“I'm in a hurry, Dick,” then-Sen. Barack Obama (D-Illinois) told Durbin, who said it would only take a minute.

“You've got to run for president,” Durbin told the future 44th president. “You're young enough that if you lose, you get another chance. But you've got something, buddy, that I've never seen in anybody.”

Obama had other people in his ear encouraging him to launch a presidential campaign after not quite two years as a senator, but Durbin was the only senator making that call publicly and privately. Two years later they were back in Chicago and Obama made history with his sweeping 2008 victory.

Durbin recalled that moment with Obama during a taping of The Washington Sun Cast video podcast that covered a 44-year career spanning a productive 14 years in the House followed by three decades in the Senate.

Advising people at the top became his forte. Durbin, 81, who is retiring in early January, ends his career as the longest serving party whip in Senate history, 22 straight years as the No. 2 leader behind Harry M. Reid (D-Nevada) and Chuck Schumer (D-New York).

He has served on the Senate Judiciary Committee for three decades, including confirmation hearings for eight of the nine Supreme Court justices. The past six years he has served as chair or ranking Democrat on the panel.

And he learned how to navigate around ambitious personalities from his first days in Congress, when a group of nearly 80 incoming House freshmen for the class of 1982 met during orientation.

Those newcomers included a young Reid, future Republican presidential nominee John McCain (R-Arizona), future governors such as Mike DeWine (R-Ohio), John Kasich (R-Ohio) and Bill Richardson (D-New Mexico).

Durbin got elected as the head of the Democratic class, along with his longtime friend and future senator, Barbara Boxer (D-California), while McCain headed up the Republican class.

Now considered a liberal stalwart, Durbin linked arms with moderates in those days to work on issues like balancing the budget. “Tip O'Neill at the time viewed most of us as traitors and kind of kept an eye on us,” he said of the House speaker.

It was a different era when power was consolidated with committee and subcommittee chairs, not in the leadership suites where it resides in today’s Congress. So Durbin’s most passionate cause at the time — fighting smoking after his father died from lung cancer at 53 — ran up against several different power brokers who represented tobacco states or were chain smokers themselves.

His first step was to ban cigarette smoking on flights, against the wishes of Democratic and Republican leaders. “Nobody had beaten big tobacco. But the folks on the other side didn't count on the fact that the House of Representatives was the largest frequent flyer club in America and they were sick and tired of secondhand smoke,” Durbin recalled.

His final move required getting past the legendary House Rules Committee chair, Rep. Claude Pepper (D-Florida), who shocked the young Durbin by ruling his amendment into a package that went to the House floor.

Pepper privately explained afterward that his greatest accomplishment was creating the National Cancer Institute and he would join Durbin in his battle. The tobacco industry has been on the run ever since.

“When I took this issue on, 29% of high school students in America smoked tobacco cigarettes — 29%! Today it's 2%. This has changed the world,” Durbin said.

After Bill Clinton won the 1992 presidential campaign and plucked Leon Panetta (D-California) out of the House to become budget director, Rep. George Miller (D-California) needed a new roommate to fill out his townhouse that had become a hub for rising star Democrats. Durbin got tapped, joining Schumer for about two decades of roommate status and periodic jockeying over who would win which leadership post.

In 1996 Durbin’s mentor, Paul Simon (D-Illinois), retired from the Senate. Durbin jumped into a crowded primary and blew away the field, eventually winning the general election by almost 16 points.

He won the next four reelection battles by double-digit margins, helping cement Illinois’ reputation as a Democratic stronghold.

His greatest honor, yet his greatest disappointment, came on the DREAM Act, legislation he crafted 25 years ago to grant permanent legal status to undocumented immigrants brought here as young children who then grew up in the United States.

A few Democrats and almost all Republicans voted to block consideration of the legislation in December 2010, when dozens of Dreamers had filled the public gallery hoping for the act’s passage. He told them later that day that he would not give up, and Obama did sign an executive order implementing parts of his law. Durbin will pass that torch to several younger Democrats when he leaves in January.
Dick Durbin, Dream Act (4896x3264, AR: 1.50)Far from the House moderate of the 1980s, in the Senate, Durbin gained a quick reputation as a liberal who could be a sharp partisan when he felt the need, particularly on the Judiciary Committee. The confirmation battles over judges in the late Clinton years and the early years of George W. Bush’s presidency set the stage for rules changes that would be implemented by Reid and future Republican majority leaders, using the “nuclear option” to ease filibuster constraints.



Not long before the former majority leader died five years ago, Durbin said he and Reid spoke about their decision to take the first party-line step to break filibuster constraints in 2013.



“He was warned ahead of time there would be retribution. It all occurred and we're still suffering from that. Harry, before he passed away, he and I talked about it. He said the Senate will never be the same,” Durbin said, adding that Reid felt “he had no choice” but to do it.



He’s careful not to tell his current colleagues what they should do in the future. But he’s not very supportive of trying to further blow up the institutional guardrails in order to do things now demanded by the party’s most liberal faithful, such as expanding the Supreme Court.



If he were chairing the Judiciary Committee next year and President Donald Trump had the chance to nominate a new justice, Durbin seems inclined to not block the nominee the way Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) blocked the 2016 nomination of Merrick Garland.



At least hold a hearing, he thinks, and vote the nominee down.



Durbin’s biggest complaint, one that would take an uprising from rank-and-file on both sides of the aisle to fix, is that too much power has been concentrated in the “four corners, whatever you want to call it.”



That’s the House speaker, House minority leader, Senate majority leader and Senate minority leader, who often at the end of a legislative session make calls about what legislation gets tacked on to some must-pass bill.



Part of the problem comes from rank-and-file lawmakers in both chambers afraid of their political shadows asking party leaders to save them from having to take tough votes on amendments, leading to a bottled-up process.



“The notion that the next vote's gonna cost you the next election is an exaggeration,” Durbin said. “I've cast 17,000 votes in the House and the Senate. I decided a long time ago I got plenty of votes for anybody to hang me with if they wish.”



But it’s also a function of power-hungry party leaders. “It's no longer up to the body on the floor, it's up to a handful of leaders in rooms that I don't have access to,” he said.



How does the second-in-command not have access to those decisions?



“It’s a great piece of real estate,” he said of an office that for 22 years sat directly above Reid and Schumer’s in the northwest wing of the Capitol.



Durbin said that his decision to retire came from his “degree in geriatrics,” watching several colleagues over the years stick around too long.



He’s ready to retire without any real regrets.



“There reaches a point when you're just not as on the ball as you once were. I did not want to reach that point and be in the middle of a Senate term,” he said. “I wanted to walk out the front door of this great institution rather than be carried out the back.”

entries.title: Brad Lander Detained By Israeli Soldiers While Harvesting Olives in the West Bank
entries.summary: A few hours after being taken into custody, Lander said he’d been released with a “warning.”
entries.content:
A New York congressional candidate was detained by the Israel Defense Forces while harvesting olives in the West Bank on Wednesday.

Brad Lander, a Democrat running to represent the state’s 10th Congressional District, was briefly taken into custody while volunteering alongside Rabbis for Human Rights, an Israeli nonprofit that advocates for social justice.

A few hours after announcing his detainment, Lander said he’d been released from IDF custody with a “warning.”

In a video statement before the incident, Lander said, “The Palestinians whose land this is have a right to harvest it in peace.”’

A photo of Lander being detained shows him standing between two IDF officers.

He and other volunteers were in the West Bank to shine a light on a recent spate of violence perpetrated against Palestinians by Israeli settlers now living in the territory, which many critics — including Lander — have referred to as an “occupation.”
https://x.com/bradlander/status/2112900551646065073?s=20According to the United Nations Human Rights Office of the High Commissioner, there were 178 attacks on olive farms in 2025, and more than 6,000 trees and saplings were damaged or destroyed.

In September 2026, Israeli military authorities issued orders to remove vegetation from roughly 339,000 square meters throughout the northern and central occupied West Bank, the U.N. reported, including the uprooting of olive trees.

"The olive harvest is an essential source of food, income and livelihood for thousands of Palestinian families, and is deeply rooted in Palestinian cultural and agricultural heritage," the U.N. said.

Lander confirmed he’d been detained in a post on X, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers.

“We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim in the West Bank,” wrote Lander. “The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”

Lander announced he was in the West Bank in a social media post on Oct. 19, saying he was assisting in the harvest with the “Protect the Harvest” coalition.

The coalition helps Palestinian farmers harvest “in the face of state-sanctioned settler terrorism,” wrote Lander.

Lander previously served as the New York City comptroller between 2022 and 2025. The Washington Sun has contacted representatives for Lander and the IDF for comment.

entries.title: Former Montgomery County Public Schools Student Alleges Antisemitic Harassment in a Federal Complaint
entries.summary: The complaint accuses MCPS of failing to protect an Orthodox Jewish student at Montgomery Blair High School.
entries.content:
A recent Montgomery County Public Schools graduate filed a federal complaint alleging that the system failed to mitigate years of antisemitic harassment against him, including a telephoned bomb threat.

The complaint, filed by the Louis D. Brandeis Center for Human Rights Under Law, accuses MCPS of violating Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin in federally funded programs. It references two executive orders, signed by President Donald Trump, affirming that antisemitism falls under the purview of Title VI as a form of ancestry-based discrimination.

The unnamed Orthodox Jewish student faced online harassment and in-person ostracization during his senior year at Montgomery Blair High School in Silver Spring, Maryland, according to the complaint. The complaint also alleges that the student received a bomb threat from a blocked caller while he was home with his siblings. Immediately after the caller hung up, fireworks were set off outside the student’s home.

The student met with his principal to discuss the harassment. While the complaint acknowledges that the school provided “some protection” to the student, it did not address the hostile environment generated by the discrimination. The student “continued to fear confrontation or physical harm, left school early when overwhelmed, and attended as little as possible.”

The complaint situated the student’s experience within a broader pattern of antisemitic discrimination across MCPS. In May, antisemitic graffiti was found spray-painted onto the wall and roof of Greenwood Elementary School. In September, a student found a swastika drawn on a desk at Walter Johnson High School. Following that incident, 40 rabbis signed a letter urging the MCPS Board of Education to address the “current crisis of skyrocketing school-based antisemitism” in the district.

The Brandeis Center called for MCPS to review the handling of the student’s complaints, issue a statement condemning antisemitic harassment, and mandate training for faculty and education for students regarding antisemitism. It also requested that MCPS incorporate the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism, which deems certain criticisms of Zionism or Israel to be antisemitic, into district policy.

“Montgomery County Public Schools is aware of the complaint filed with the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights,” a spokesperson for MCPSwrote in a statement to The Washington Sun. “As this is an ongoing matter, we are unable to provide further comment at this time.”

entries.title: Trump Blamed Muslim Migrants for the French Riots. Macron Says That's 'Stupid.'
entries.summary: The French president says there “has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath” of the looting in Paris and other cities.
entries.content:
By Samuel Petrequin

French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that foreign leaders — including those “on the other side of the Atlantic” — are trying to exploit France's tense social climate for their own political agenda.

Protests over soaring living costs have led to widespread rioting and looting in France.

U.S. President Donald Trump has used the violence to rally his political supporters, making unsubstantiated claims that Muslim migrants are responsible for the unrest, and urging Macron to “close your borders and take control before it is too late!”

Macron responded by saying there “has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath” of the looting in Paris and other French cities last weekend.

“And that has led to comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said.

Asked by a reporter if he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.”

Macron then added that there have been "AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.”

Macron did not specify which AI-generated images he was referring to, nor how he knew the content was false. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said its office can provide the countries concerned with the necessary clarification, “to help them avoid spreading or amplifying false information and making baseless claims on social media.”

Macron and Trump once enjoyed a good relationship but Trump regularly mocks the French president in his public speeches.

“The fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country," Macron said. “So those people really bother me.”

“When I see leaders who are in the middle of election campaigns, whether in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic — who sometimes naively repeat AI-generated content or spread narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote about what happened in France — they’re using our country for their own political campaigns," said Macron. "And we don’t need that.”

Macron was speaking in Qatar at the end of a tour of key energy suppliers in Gulf Arab states, where he secured an additional 100,000 metric tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates, with a further 100,000 tons to be confirmed in Bahrain.

Macron's office said he traveled to the Middle East to find solutions to the energy crisis and rising energy prices, and to secure supplies of oil, gas, diesel and jet fuel.

The Elysee said nearly 295,000 additional tons of diesel per month could be secured, including volumes from Saudi Arabia, equivalent to more than 10% of France's monthly diesel consumption.

entries.title: How Rough Is It for Republicans? Look at This North Carolina District.
entries.summary: The state’s once safe 11th District is slipping. “Based on early voting, it is a likely Democratic district,” a Republican strategist said.
entries.content:
North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District sits in a rural and conservative region of the state, has been held by a Republican for more than a decade and backed Donald Trump by a nearly double-digit margin in 2024.

And right now, it might be on the verge of turning blue in November.

Republicans are in serious danger of losing a once safe seat in the 11th District, according to more than a dozen interviews with local and national political operatives from both parties. They described the race between Democrat Jamie Ager and Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom as teetering toward Democratic control for months, thanks to what one local Democratic official called a “perfect storm” of problems for Republicans both locally and nationally.

Republicans in the district suffered a blow over the summer when incumbent Rep. Chuck Edwards was forced to end his campaign under scandal. He was censured by Congress in early September following a House ethics investigation.

Conditions for the party deteriorated further this fall, as Trump’s poll numbers slid nationally and the Republican nominee for Senate in North Carolina, Michael Whatley, struggled to gain traction at the top of the ticket.

Some Republicans fear that with less than two weeks to go, the race is already lost.

“The bad environment in North Carolina, combined with a dead top of the ticket and a scandal with the incumbent made this a long shot to hold onto this cycle,” said one Republican strategist who works on House races, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “They probably knew that in September but fought it out as long as they could.”

In a sign of the party’s growing skepticism about their chances in the district, No Going Back PAC, a Trump-controlled super PAC, on Tuesday canceled future ad reservations in the district, a source familiar with the group confirmed to The Washington Sun. (The spending cut was first reported by Punchbowl News.)

Other Republican groups, like the National Republican Congressional Committee, are still slated to spend in the district over the next two weeks, but party operatives are increasingly skeptical that they can salvage a win. Balkcom’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment about the race.

“I actually think the rating in the 11th District should be likely Democrat, not lean Democrat,” said one North Carolina Republican strategist, given anonymity to speak candidly about the race. “Based on early voting, it is a likely Democratic district.”

At a rally in Greenville, North Carolina, on Tuesday, Trump suggested that both Balkcom and Laurie Buckhout, the Republican candidate for the 1st District, were going to have “close races,” requiring a “special call out” from the president.

The Republican strategist said they expected that Rep. Richard Hudson’s race in the central part of the state, considered a safe Republican seat, would likely be more competitive on Election Day, despite it being viewed as a safe seat for the GOP for most of the cycle. Hudson recently began spending on TV advertising, and the Democratic super PAC House Majority PAC has identified the race to donors as a potential target.

The GOP’s troubles in the 11th District are both a sign of how deeply Democrats might reach into formerly red terrain — Democratic operatives are increasingly confident about their chances in an array of seats Trump won by double digits — and a confluence of local factors that have made the seat uniquely tough for Republicans.

Edwards’ sudden departure left Republicans in a bind. The party had to quickly choose a new candidate after Edwards dropped out of the race following allegations that he was sexually harassing women on his congressional staff. It gave Balkcom little time — less than three months — to introduce herself to the voters across the district, which spans 16 rugged, mountainous counties.

“When we're out here talking to people, there are still people who are like, ‘Well, wait, what happened to Chuck?” said a Republican Party volunteer in western North Carolina who was given anonymity to speak candidly.

Margaret Ackiss, a member at large of the 11th District’s Republican Party who nominated Balkcom to run for the seat, described the fallout from Edwards’ scandal and late-stage dropout as resulting in a “sad state of affairs.” Balkcom’s path to winning would require balancing getting her name out in rural counties like Cherokee, Clay, Graham, Macon and Swain — the reddest parts of the region — while attempting to win unaffiliated voters near the district’s population center, Ackiss said.

“The outer rim of far western North Carolina, they have no idea who she is,” Ackiss said.

Democratic campaign operatives in Washington consider Ager one of their best recruits of the cycle. Ager has deep family roots in the district and styles himself as a “Mountain Democrat” not beholden to his party.

“The number one thing I think that’s made this competitive is Jamie Ager,” said Grayson Barnette, who is managing Ager’s campaign.

The GOP’s troubles, the national momentum for Democrats and Ager’s appeal have made local Democrats feel confident about flipping the seat.

“All of these things have just come together for a perfect storm for 2026, and that's what makes us optimistic,” said Beth Jones, Democratic chair of the 11th District.

National Democrats have been bullish on Ager’s chances for months, considering him more likely to win than many of the party’s other candidates in competitive races. One Democratic strategist gave Ager a “90%” chance of winning; another operative said they had already mentally put his race in the win column.

Some Republicans are holding out hope for Balkcom, saying that they think the race has tightened in recent weeks. Vice President JD Vance visited the district Monday to rally Republicans, in a boost to Balkcom.

“NC-11 is a Republican district, Jennifer Balkcom is a phenomenal candidate with deep local roots, and liberal Jamie Ager is a partisan Democrat whose radical tax-and-spend policies firmly align him with the Democratic Socialist extremists engaging in a hostile takeover of his party,” said Reilly Richardson, a NRCC spokesperson, in a statement. “Voters know Ager would make their lives more expensive and less safe, which is why they’ll turn out for Jennifer Balkcom.”

Some local Republicans still believe the district is a tough place for a Democrat to escape the party’s battered reputation, especially on cultural issues.

“What the Democrat Party stands for just doesn't align with the values that are deeply held by the people here,” said Merry Guy, chair of the District 11 GOP. “And I'm talking about some of those good old blue dog Democrats, too — their party has left them, and they know that.”

The district’s Republican representatives, though, have had trouble for years. Edwards’ predecessors faced scandals of their own. Former Rep. Madison Cawthorn’s time in Congress was plagued by multiple run-ins with the law and allegations that he sexually harassed college classmates. Cawthorn’s predecessor, former White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, was held in contempt of Congress for not complying with a subpoena from the House select committee, which was investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol.

If this district flips next month, the 2024 election results serve as foreshadowing. Nine counties in the district moved slightly leftward in 2024 as a majority of the state and country moved to the right.

“It's a Republican-leaning district, but it is an election year where that may get wiped out,” said longtime Republican political consultant Carter Wrenn. He added that the dominant factor in the race is Trump rather than either candidate’s strengths.

“It’s in Trump’s hands,” Wrenn said.

Right now, the trends are not in the GOP’s favor. The war in Iran remains unpopular, and rising gas prices are frustrating voters. Economic pressures in the 11th District are compounded by what’s been a slow recovery process after Hurricane Helene ravaged the district in 2024.

Republicans are also concerned that Whatley, their Senate candidate, will stunt the success of others downballot. Whatley entered the race with Trump’s endorsement but has consistently trailed in polls to former Gov. Roy Cooper.

“Michael Whatley will be an albatross on everyone below him on the ballot, and that could’ve been controlled if President Trump would’ve kept his thumb off the scale,” said Michele Woodhouse, a former Republican chair of the 11th District.

entries.title: Russia Frees American Prisoner During Visit by Steve Witkoff
entries.summary: Stephen Hubbard was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison following a closed trial.
entries.content:
By Dasha Litvinova and Eric Tucker

Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, in a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.

Trump said in a Truth Social post that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call last week to free Stephen Hubbard, and that, unlike previous releases, his had not required the U.S. to give up anyone in return.

“Welcome home, Stephen, it’s great to have you back,” Trump said.

Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan, was on his way home following a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who also held talks with Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.

Hubbard was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison following a closed trial. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv's forces until being captured two months later. The U.S. government under the Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.

The release came amid Trump moves to benefit Russia


Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he's going home to his family.”

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media on Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was “raised by the American side for a certain time,” and Putin decided to free the man out of “humanitarian considerations.”

He added that general contacts "continue on a regular basis between the intelligence services.”

The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin.

Those include Trump's decision last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war. That reversal followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections.

Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks Wednesday with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg.

Other Americans remain jailed in Russia

Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer.

Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the only one designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners.

Global Reach, a group that works to free Americans detained abroad and currently represents five American held in Russia, praised the release but called for the other prisoners to come home as well.

“We are grateful to the Trump Administration for reuniting Stephen Hubbard with his family, but at the same time, we know that there are five other families of Americans held in Russia who are going to have a hard time understanding why their loved one was not included in the deal,” Eric Lebson, the group's chief strategy officer, said in a statement.

Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus.

The organization in August posted an open letter to Trump that it said was written by Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, in which she offered praise for Trump but also said her brother had been subjected to “constant beatings, torture and starvation” while in custody.

“Even so, everything that you’re doing isn’t going to matter to my kidnapped, American Veteran brother, Stephen James Hubbard (soon to be 74) if Putin won’t cave and let him come home and he dies up there in a Nazi prison (crying),” the letter said.

entries.title: Supreme Court Keeps Freeze on Limits for Transgender Inmate Care
entries.summary: The brief order maintains a lower court judge’s freeze on a Trump administration policy banning hormone therapy and other treatments in federal prisons.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday denied the Trump administration’s attempt to halt gender-affirming care for inmates in federal prison while a legal challenge plays out.

The court’s unsigned, two-sentence order maintains a lower court judge’s freeze on a Federal Bureau of Prisons policy banning hormone therapy and other treatments for transgender people in federal prisons and immigration detention centers.

The order notes that Justice Clarence Thomas and Justice Samuel Alito would have granted the administration’s application to put the previous ruling on hold and allow the policy to take effect while the litigation proceeds.

Had the court ruled in the administration’s favor, many of the roughly 2,000 federal inmates who identify as transgender could have lost access to a range of treatments that have long been available to them.

The Bureau of Prisons, which oversees the nation’s 153,000 federal inmates, issued the most recent version of the policy in February, seeking a near-total ban on gender-affirming care.

In addition to targeting hormone therapy, it sought to prohibit surgeries and social accommodations such as clothing, cosmetics and chest binders. It also seeks to remove a general requirement that prison staffers use an inmate's preferred pronouns.

As an alternative, the new policy proposes providing inmates psychotherapy and psychotropic medication.

Previous policies allowed surgeries, hormones and social support for inmates who were transitioning.

The American Civil Liberties Union and other advocacy groups sued on behalf of several inmates with gender dysphoria last year, arguing that the new policy violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishments. The lawsuit, which was brought in Washington, D.C., also alleges violations of administrative law.

U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth certified a class of plaintiffs that includes all people who are or will be in Bureau of Prisons custody “who are or will be diagnosed with gender dysphoria.” He issued multiple rulings blocking the policy, finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed at least on their claim that the government didn’t take legally required steps in developing it.

The Trump administration went to the Supreme Court last month seeking an emergency order blocking Lamberth’s order. Government lawyers argued that blocking the policy nationwide would pose unspecified “security and prison-administrative concerns.”

Executive branch officials needed particularly broad leeway to independently make decisions about treatment for gender dysphoria “in the context of prison administration,” government lawyers argued in their application.

The government said inmates would still be provided “appropriate, individualized treatment for gender dysphoria, while disallowing only interventions that are medically unnecessary.”

In response, the ACLU contended that granting the government’s request would overturn a “three-decades long status quo” under which prison officials provided hormone treatment for people who entered federal custody already receiving such care.

The group’s brief said the prisons bureau had ignored its own data on transgender care when developing the new policy in violation of federal administrative law.

The ACLU also said the prisons bureau had not pointed to “a single security incident relating to its provision of this treatment over the past 30 years, and it does not ban other types of medical care that actually do present security issues.”

“Had BOP’s doctors found this treatment unhelpful or harmful to patients or had the agency found that the treatment compromised security, surely BOP would have mentioned it in the administrative record,” the ACLU said.

entries.title: George W. Bush’s Brother Backs Talarico and Bashes Ken Paxton
entries.summary: Neil Bush is the second member of his family to come out in support of the Democratic Senate candidate in the past week.
entries.content:
Neil Bush, the brother of former President George W. Bush, said this week that he voted for James Talarico, breaking with his family’s Republican political dynasty.

Bush, the fourth of former President George H. W. Bush and first lady Barbara Bush’s six children, announced that he voted for the Democrat in a Facebook post on Tuesday, acknowledging the difficulty of the decision.

“I have never posted a political message on Facebook, not wanting to offend friends whose views may be very different than mine,” he wrote.

Bush said he voted for the candidate because he is deeply concerned about Ken Paxton’s record, and he has “genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico,” including integrity, civility, humility and a willingness to listen to those with whom he disagrees.

Paxton, Talarico’s opponent, has served as Texas attorney general since 2015. In 2020, he challenged the results of the presidential election in an attempt to help President Donald Trump remain in power.

“I believe that effort was an affront to our democratic institutions and the peaceful transfer of power,” Bush wrote in his social media post.

Paxton was also impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 for allegedly misusing his office to help a friend and donor who was under federal investigation. He was later acquitted by the Texas Senate.

Bush said he’s worried about a political culture that pledges loyalty to an individual and doesn’t hold people in power accountable for their actions.

“I believe Donald Trump and those who have enabled him have done enormous damage to the Republican Party,” Bush continued.

Bush did not state whether he’s permanently breaking with the Republican Party but said he voted “against a style of politics that I believe has damaged our country.”

He continued: “More importantly, I voted for the kind of character and leadership I hope will help heal it.”

Bush added that he continues to believe in many traditional Republican principles.

Bush is the second member of his family to support Talarico. Barbara Bush, the daughter of former president George W. Bush, donated $2,500 to a political action committee supporting Talarico, Texas Public Radio reported.

entries.title: DOJ Watchdog Declines to Probe Jeanine Pirro’s Reflecting Pool Prosecution
entries.summary: David Hearn's team argues that the watchdog is uniquely positioned to dig into allegations of misconduct against the government officials involved in the case.
entries.content:
By Eric Tucker

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Justice's inspector general has declined to investigate the handling of the criminal case against a former Olympian cleared of accusations that he intentionally damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, according to a letter Wednesday from the man's lawyers.

The internal watchdog told David Hearn's lawyers that the allegations of professional misconduct that they made fall outside its jurisdiction and are instead within the purview of the department's Office of Professional Responsibility, according to the letter, which urges Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume to reconsider the decision.

“Given the substantial public attention devoted to this matter, and the significant questions raised concerning the conduct of federal officials, declining independent review would risk undermining public confidence in the Department’s ability to police its own conduct. Such a result would be inconsistent with the purposes for which Congress established the OIG and would be a betrayal of its mission,” the letter says.

Hearn's lawyers this month had asked for investigations by the inspectors general at the departments of Justice and Interior, citing a broad variety of “incompetence and misconduct” that they said occurred during the criminal investigation and prosecution of their client. They say they believe they have identified potential crimes in the Trump administration's handling of the case, including witness tampering, obstruction of justice and the subornation of false testimony.

The Justice Department moved to dismiss the case last summer, saying newly produced evidence from the Interior Department showed that Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, was not responsible for damage to the pool’s lining. A District of Columbia judge later permanently threw out the prosecution.

Hearn’s lawyers said in their initial letter to the watchdogs that the evidence that established their client’s innocence had been in the Justice Department’s possession for weeks and was “simply ignored.” They asked the inspectors general to investigate why prosecutors “rushed to indict” under what they said was pressure from Republican President Donald Trump, who had launched a massive renovation project of the Reflecting Pool for the celebration in Washington of America's 250th anniversary.

In renewing their request for an inspector general investigation, Hearn's team argues that the watchdog is uniquely positioned — both in terms of tools and independence — to dig into allegations of misconduct against the government officials involved in the case.

They note that unlike the inspector general's office, the Office of Professional Responsibility, which also investigates some categories of professional misconduct, reports to the deputy attorney general and attorney general and has no obligation to publicize its work or report its findings to Congress.

Hearn's lawyers also say the inspector general is the right office to investigate the potential criminal misconduct they believe they have identified within the government, asserting that prosecutors elicited false testimony from a witness who testified before the grand jury and violated Hearn's civil rights by proceeding with a flawed criminal case. They say the inspector general should investigate whether U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, whose office handled the case, violated ethical rules in a news conference when she announced charges against Hearn.

The U.S. attorney's office did not respond to a request seeking comment when Hearn's attorneys raised the allegations earlier this month.

Among Hearn's attorneys is Michael Bromwich, a Justice Department inspector general during the Clinton administration.

“In a case such as this one, when some of the allegations directly involve the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia, there is substantial reason to question whether any meaningful independent review would occur,” the lawyers' letter says. “Your decision not to investigate would be consigning these serious allegations to oblivion despite the enormous public interest in the matter and the absence thus far of any accountability for the individuals involved.”

entries.title: Maryland Fires Football Coach Mike Locksley After Eight Seasons
entries.summary: The Terrapins had lost their last 12 Big Ten games.
entries.content:
The University of Maryland fired head football coach Mike Locksley on Wednesday, ending his eight-season tenure leading the program.

The Washington, D.C., native finished his time with the Terps with a 39-54 overall record. Despite leading Maryland to three consecutive bowl wins from 2021-23, his teams never won more than eight games in a season. Things had gotten particularly dire the last few seasons, with his team losing 20 of its last 22 Big Ten games.

On Saturday, Maryland dropped to 2-5 after squandering an early lead in a 37-30 home loss to Rutgers.

Locksley was paid $6.4 million this season and was under contract through 2028. In light of his termination, the school owes him a buyout worth more than $9 million.

The Terps hired Locksley in December 2018 in the aftermath of the death of offensive lineman Jordan McNair from heatstroke earlier in the year, which led to the firing of head coach D.J. Durkin.

Locksley was largely effective in helping to move the program past the Durkin era and earned high marks for his ability to recruit from the DMV area and add talent through the transfer portal. But that did not result in positive results on the field.

Replacing Locksley will fall to Maryland athletic director Jim Smith, who’ll be leading a hiring search for a new football coach for the first time. Hired in July 2025, Smith previously spent five years with the MLB’s Atlanta Braves as senior vice president of business strategy, and before that he ran the Ohio State Alumni Association.

Co-defensive coordinator Aazaar Abdul-Rahim will be the Terps interim coach, according to The Athletic’s Bruce Feldman. Abdul-Rahim, another local, was the head coach at Friendship Collegiate Academy in D.C. before jumping to the college ranks.

entries.title: Flock Camera Company Adds Federal Lobbying Firepower
entries.summary: The company is facing scrutiny over its surveillance technology, which is used by law enforcement across the country.
entries.content:
Flock Safety hired two new lobbying firms and significantly increased its federal lobbying spending in recent months as backlash to its AI-powered vehicle-surveillance technology boiled over.

Flock spent $360,000 lobbying federal lawmakers and regulators from the beginning of July through the end of September, up from $210,000 during the same period in 2025, according to new disclosures filed this week under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

In mid-August, the company also hired a team of Democratic lobbyists at Invariant and others from the boutique Republican lobbying firm Off Hill Strategies.

Invariant reported receiving $90,000 through the end of September to “educate policymakers about the use of public safety technology,” and Off Hill Strategies received $50,000 to lobby on “appropriate federal guardrails for ALPR technology.”

The company is facing increasing scrutiny from Congress for its extensive data collection system and misuse by law enforcement that’s led in some cases to false accusations.

A Flock spokesperson said the company backs further regulations.

“For more than four years, Flock has been at the table with policymakers supporting stronger regulations around the use of license plate reader technology,” Paris Lewbel, a spokesperson for Flock, wrote in a statement to The Washington Sun. “We believe in thoughtful, bipartisan legislation that puts strong privacy, transparency, and accountability measures in place.”

Dozens of cities and counties across the country, including Arlington County, Virginia, have paused or canceled contracts with Flock since July, according to the advocacy group DeFlock the USA.

At a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing last month, Chair Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) and other lawmakers called for legislation to place guardrails on the technology and expressed frustration that executives at Flock and other companies had not accepted the committee’s invitations to testify.

The addition of Invariant and Off Hill Strategies to Flock’s lobbying roster bolstered its existing influence operation. Flock hired its first federal lobbying firms, BGR Government Affairs and Mercury Public Affairs, in December 2024, just before Trump took office, and spent $840,000 on federal lobbying in 2025.

BGR reported receiving $90,000 to “provide strategic counsel and advocate on issues related to public safety and security” with Congress, the White House, the Justice Department and the Department of Transportation. Mercury Public Affairs reported receiving $120,000 to lobby Congress and the White House Office of Administration on safety and security issues.

Flock also paid Modern Fortis $10,000 to lobby the Justice Department on “utilization of LPR cameras,” the lobbying firm recently reported. Carlough Solutions reported receiving $20,000 to lobby the House specifically on issues related to public safety and security in the fiscal year 2027 appropriations bill.

“Engaging with federal lawmakers is a natural extension of that commitment, and we will continue to support efforts to establish clear, meaningful safeguards for public safety technology,” Lewbel said in the statement.
